hero.lead: An island nation of 32.7 million that grows more of the world’s vanilla than any other, and where three in four citizens live below the poverty line.

register.name: Integrated Urban Development and Resilience Project for Jobs (PRODUIRE2)
register.note: Climate-resilient infrastructure for about 1.5 million people
register.text: Flood protection, drainage, solid waste and land titles in Greater Antananarivo, and 20,000 homes rebuilt to resilient standards in Greater Toamasina, with schools and health facilities. About 17,000 jobs and land documents for 50,000 parcels are expected, at least 40% of them naming women.

register.name: Improving Nutrition Outcomes Program, additional financing
register.detail: Announced 8 June 2026 · $80 million IDA · $10 million Global Financing Facility grant
register.note: Health and nutrition services for more than 5 million people
register.text: Scales up maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health and nutrition services in the most vulnerable regions, with facility upgrades and more health workers. The programme aims to reach 600,000 children by 2028 and to cut child stunting by 30 percent.

register.name: Accelerating Sustainable and Clean Energy Access Transformation (ASCENT Madagascar)
register.detail: Announced 6 May 2026 · Program-for-Results, the first in Madagascar
register.note: Electricity for more than 2.5 million people by 2030
register.text: 200,000 new JIRAMA household connections, solar and batteries for 30 isolated power centres, 312,500 off-grid connections and 1.5 million clean or improved cooking appliances. Clean cooking is the standard that holds Madagascar’s Coverage at 2; each tranche is paid on verified results.

register.name: Madagascar Multimodal Transport and Logistics Project
register.note: Rail, ports, the Pangalanes Canal and airports, for about 3.8 million people
register.text: Rehabilitates key sections of the 371 km railway from Antananarivo to the port of Toamasina, the ports of Majunga and Tulear, about 200 km of the Pangalanes Canal and three regional airports. Coastal traders, fishers and tourism businesses gain year-round, cyclone-resilient access to markets.

register.name: Cyclone payouts after Fytia and Gezani
register.detail: Reported 2 April 2026 · REPAIR $19.9 million · ARC insurance about $5.6 million · Replica cover $3.79 million
register.note: Rapid funds after the cyclones of February 2026
register.text: Pre-arranged finance paid out after the cyclones of February 2026: reserves of the World Bank’s REPAIR programme, supported by the Global Shield Financing Facility, and African Risk Capacity parametric insurance, with replica cover for humanitarian partners. The REPAIR reserves were drawn first, for the early response.

register.name: Second Equitable and Resilient Growth Development Policy Operation
register.detail: Announced 18 June 2025 · IDA · The second of a series of three
register.note: Budget support for reforms in telecoms, energy, mining and public finance
register.text: Supports the opening of the telecoms market, a stronger JIRAMA with fewer power cuts, a new Mining Code and the removal of some tax incentives in the 2025 budget. Internet prices have fallen since new operators entered the market.

register.name: Extended Credit Facility and Resilience and Sustainability Facility
register.detail: Approved 21 June 2024 · 36 months · ECF SDR 256.62 million · RSF SDR 244.4 million · Third and fourth reviews completed 30 September 2026
register.note: About $155 million made available on 30 September 2026
register.text: The ECF (about $337 million) supports fiscal sustainability, governance and human capital; the RSF (about $321 million) finances climate adaptation, disaster resilience and ecosystem protection. The combined reviews of September 2026 released SDR 114.052 million, about $155 million, during the political transition.

register.name: Digital and Energy Connectivity for Inclusion in Madagascar
register.text: Extends electricity and digital connectivity to underserved areas.

register.name: Rural Livelihoods Productivity and Resilience Project
register.text: Raises the productivity and resilience of rural livelihoods.

register.name: Madagascar Safety Nets and Resilience Project
register.text: Supports the poorest households and their resilience to shocks.

register.name: Madagascar National Water Project
register.text: Extends water supply where just over half of citizens have a basic service.

register.name: Pandemic Preparedness and Basic Health Services Delivery Project
register.note: Basic health services; coverage 33 on the WHO index
register.text: Strengthens basic health services, where coverage stands at 33 on the WHO index.

register.name: Least-Cost Electricity Access Development Project (LEAD)
register.text: Expands access to electricity at least cost.

register.name: Financial Management and Economic Resilience Support Programme, Phase II
register.detail: Announced 26 May 2026 · ADF loan $27.2 million · Transition Support Facility loan $40.8 million
register.note: Second phase of a $136 million programme
register.text: Supports public financial management and private sector competitiveness, an independent electricity regulator, a National Fund for Sustainable Energy for off-grid and rural power, and a modern public-private partnership law. Tax revenue is projected to rise from 10.5% to 12% of GDP by the end of 2026.

register.name: IFC loan to Groupe Talys
register.detail: Announced 24 April 2026 · Long-term loan · Sanifer and Kibo
register.text: Finances Sanifer, the largest importer and distributor of construction materials in Madagascar, and the Kibo cash-and-carry stores. Madagascar is short of about two million homes, a deficit that grows by more than 100,000 a year; up to 14,000 indirect jobs are expected.

register.name: IFC local-currency loan to BNI Madagascar
register.detail: Announced 9 January 2025 · In ariary · IDA Private Sector Window first-loss guarantee
register.text: Lends in ariary to micro, small and medium enterprises, including informal entrepreneurs, through one of the largest banks in Madagascar. The formal finance gap for small firms is 24% of GDP, against 19% across sub-Saharan Africa.
